title: Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma: From Past to Future—A Comprehensive Review of Pathophysiology and Therapeutic Advances

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution, Classification, and Epidemiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Historical Evolution, Classification, and Epidemiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) occupies a distinctive place in hematologic oncology because its clinical history mirrors the broader evolution of cancer medicine: a disease once associated with near-uniform fatality has become highly curable in many patients through advances in pathology, staging, radiotherapy, and multi-agent chemotherapy ref [16], ref [39]. Contemporary guidelines frame cHL as a biologically and clinically defined entity within Hodgkin lymphoma, emphasizing the need for accurate diagnosis, careful staging, and risk-adapted management as prerequisites for excellent outcomes ref [16], ref [39].

From a classificatory perspective, current practice distinguishes cHL from nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, reflecting differences in morphology, immunophenotype, and therapeutic approach ref [16], ref [39]. Within cHL itself, the major histologic subtypes—nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, and lymphocyte-depleted—retain epidemiologic and clinicopathologic relevance, even as modern treatment algorithms are increasingly guided by stage, bulk, symptoms, and response assessment rather than histology alone ref [16], ref [39].

Epidemiologically, Hodgkin lymphoma shows marked variation by age and geography, with cHL accounting for the great majority of cases and demonstrating a characteristic bimodal age distribution in many populations ref [16], ref [39]. These broad patterns underscore a central theme for the field: despite major therapeutic success, the burden of disease remains heterogeneous across adolescents, young adults, and older patients, and outcomes continue to depend on timely diagnosis, supportive infrastructure, and access to contemporary care ref [16], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution, Classification, and Epidemiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Historical Evolution, Classification, and Epidemiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Modern classification of Hodgkin lymphoma distinguishes classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) from nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, reflecting major advances in morphology, immunophenotyping, and biologic understanding. cHL is defined by the presence of Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg cells within a rich but ineffective inflammatory microenvironment and is further subdivided into nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, and lymphocyte-depleted variants, each associated with somewhat different clinicopathologic patterns and age distributions ref [5].

This classification framework has practical implications because cHL is not determined solely by malignant cell morphology, but also by the composition of the surrounding immune infiltrate. Studies evaluating the tumor microenvironment have shown that markers such as FOXP3, CD68, and CD20 at diagnosis carry prognostic information, underscoring that host–tumor interactions are integral to disease biology and may refine risk stratification beyond conventional histology alone ref [15]. The relevance of CD20 expression in a subset of cases also helped motivate biologically targeted approaches, including rituximab-based strategies in selected relapsed CD20-positive Hodgkin lymphoma, illustrating how classification increasingly interfaces with therapeutics ref [17].

Accurate clinical classification further depends on modern staging methods. Functional imaging with 18F-FDG PET/CT has become central to initial staging and response assessment in lymphoma, improving detection of nodal and extranodal disease compared with older anatomic approaches ref [13]. In Hodgkin lymphoma specifically, PET/CT-based evaluation of bone and bone marrow involvement may reduce the need for routine bone marrow trephine biopsy at diagnosis, highlighting the historical shift from invasive staging procedures toward imaging-driven disease characterization ref [16]. Together, these developments link pathologic classification with contemporary clinical assessment and have helped standardize cHL evaluation across treatment settings ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution, Classification, and Epidemiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Historical Evolution, Classification, and Epidemiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A critical dimension of the historical evolution of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is the recognition that therapeutic success has been accompanied by substantial long-term morbidity. As cHL transitioned from a frequently fatal disease to a highly curable malignancy, survivorship emerged as a central epidemiologic and clinical concern. Broad overviews of lymphoma diagnosis and treatment emphasize that modern disease assessment must therefore extend beyond initial remission rates to include late toxicities, functional outcomes, and survivorship care planning, particularly in younger patients with long life expectancy after cure ref [9].

Among these late effects, persistent symptom burden remains highly relevant. Longitudinal data from the German Hodgkin Study Group show that cancer-related fatigue can affect both patients undergoing treatment and long-term survivors, underscoring that epidemiologic burden is not captured fully by survival statistics alone ref [14]. This observation is especially important in cHL, where cure is common and quality-of-life impairment may persist for years after therapy, thereby shaping contemporary risk-adapted treatment strategies.

The history of cHL management also includes the challenge of relapsed disease, where curability declines and treatment intensity often increases. In this setting, stem-cell-based salvage approaches have played a major role in refining the therapeutic landscape; notably, reduced-intensity allogeneic transplantation has shown superiority over conventional treatment after relapse following autologous transplantation in selected patients, illustrating how the classification of patients by relapse status has direct prognostic and therapeutic implications ref [16]. At the same time, reports of secondary malignancies such as malignant mesothelioma after prior radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma highlight the enduring epidemiologic consequences of older treatment paradigms and the need to balance disease control with long-term safety ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution, Classification, and Epidemiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Historical Evolution, Classification, and Epidemiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Population-based registries have been central to modern epidemiologic understanding of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), particularly in defining real-world incidence, treatment patterns, and long-term outcomes outside clinical trials. National databases enable longitudinal capture of stage distribution, age structure, relapse events, and survival, thereby complementing trial cohorts that often underrepresent older adults and patients with comorbidity. In this context, the Danish National Lymphoma Registry represents an important infrastructure for contemporary lymphoma surveillance and quality assessment in routine practice [38].

Registry-based approaches are especially valuable for cHL because the disease spans distinct demographic groups and clinical contexts. They permit comparison of outcomes across adolescents and young adults, older patients, and health-system settings, and they are well suited to documenting temporal changes associated with advances in imaging, risk stratification, supportive care, and combined-modality therapy [38]. Such datasets also help clarify persistent inequities, including inferior outcomes in frail or elderly patients, whose prognosis may differ substantially from that reported in highly selected study populations.

Accordingly, epidemiologic interpretation of cHL should integrate both historical clinical trial evidence and high-quality national registry data. This dual perspective is essential for understanding how major therapeutic progress has translated into population-level cure, where gains have been uneven, and which subgroups remain priorities for future therapeutic and health-services research [38].

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution, Classification, and Epidemiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Historical Evolution, Classification, and Epidemiology of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
From an epidemiologic and clinical standpoint, classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is best understood as a highly curable but heterogeneous disease whose outcomes are shaped by age, stage, treatment access, and survivorship burden. Contemporary reviews emphasize that cHL shows a characteristic bimodal age distribution in many populations, with peaks in young adulthood and later life, while prognosis in older adults remains less favorable because of comorbidity, treatment intolerance, and biologic differences ref [16], ref [24]. These population patterns are also relevant to health systems, since disparities in diagnostic resources and protocol implementation continue to influence stage migration and survival across regions ref [25].

Risk stratification has evolved in parallel with epidemiologic understanding. In pediatric disease, the Childhood Hodgkin International Prognostic Score (CHIPS) illustrates how age-specific models can refine event-free survival prediction beyond conventional staging alone, underscoring that prognostic frameworks should not be uniformly extrapolated across age groups ref [22]. At the same time, modern staging and response-adapted strategies increasingly rely on PET/CT, which has altered how disease extent is defined and how early treatment response is interpreted, with major implications for both epidemiologic comparisons and contemporary outcome reporting ref [10].

A final epidemiologic consideration is that cHL should be distinguished from related Hodgkin entities and from its long-term survivorship consequences. Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma has distinct biology, clinical behavior, and management principles, reinforcing the importance of precise classification when interpreting incidence and survival statistics ref [15]. Moreover, as cure rates have improved, health-related quality of life has emerged as a critical population-level outcome; systematic review data show that fatigue, psychosocial effects, and treatment sequelae remain substantial even among long-term survivors ref [18]. Thus, the modern epidemiology of cHL must integrate not only incidence and survival, but also subtype specificity, age-adapted prognosis, imaging-era staging, and survivorship outcomes ref [16], ref [18].

subsections.section_title: Biological Basis and Tumor Microenvironment in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Biological Basis and Tumor Microenvironment in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is biologically distinctive because the malignant Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg (HRS) cells usually constitute only a minor fraction of the tumor mass, whereas the bulk of the lesion is composed of a reactive cellular infiltrate. This architecture underlies the disease’s pathobiology: HRS cells depend on bidirectional interactions with surrounding T cells, macrophages, eosinophils, fibroblasts, and cytokine networks for survival, proliferation, and immune escape, making the microenvironment a central component rather than a passive background ref [16], ref [39].

From a biological perspective, cHL is generally derived from crippled germinal-center B cells that have lost much of the conventional B-cell transcriptional program, yet retain the capacity to persist through aberrant activation of prosurvival signaling and microenvironmental support. The resulting tumor niche is characterized by extensive cytokine and chemokine secretion that recruits non-malignant immune cells and helps create an immunologically permissive milieu; these features have directly informed the development of modern targeted and immune-based therapies now incorporated into contemporary management frameworks ref [16], ref [39].

A further layer of pathogenesis in a subset of cases is provided by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), which contributes to lymphomagenesis through latent viral programs that promote HRS-cell survival and shape the surrounding immune contexture. EBV-positive cHL is therefore an important example of how viral oncogenesis, immune dysregulation, and tumor–microenvironment crosstalk converge in this disease, reinforcing the need to view cHL as a biologically composite malignancy rather than a tumor defined solely by its rare malignant cells ref [20], ref [16], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Biological Basis and Tumor Microenvironment in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Biological Basis and Tumor Microenvironment in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A defining biological feature of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is that the malignant Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells constitute only a minor fraction of the tumor mass, whereas the bulk is composed of a reactive but highly structured microenvironment. This cellular ecosystem includes T lymphocytes, macrophages, eosinophils, plasma cells, and variably B cells, all recruited and functionally shaped by cytokines and chemokines produced by tumor cells. As a result, cHL behaves less like a conventional high–tumor-cell-content malignancy and more like a disease in which neoplastic cells persist through active dependence on stromal and immune support ref [3].

The composition of this microenvironment is not merely descriptive, but clinically meaningful. Immunohistochemical studies have shown that markers reflecting regulatory T cells, macrophages, and background B cells carry prognostic information at diagnosis. In particular, expression patterns of FOXP3, CD68, and CD20 in the cHL microenvironment correlate with outcome, underscoring that the balance between immunoregulatory, inflammatory, and residual immune components influences disease behavior ref [15]. These observations support the concept that macrophage-rich or immunosuppressive niches can favor tumor persistence, whereas other infiltrating populations may reflect a more constrained biology.

This microenvironment-centered view has had major therapeutic implications. The dependence of cHL on nonmalignant cellular support helps explain why immune-directed strategies can be effective even when directly targeting only a small malignant compartment. More broadly, recognition of cHL as a lymphoma sustained by reciprocal signaling between Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg cells and surrounding immune cells has provided a biological foundation for subsequent development of microenvironment-modulating and checkpoint-based therapies ref [3], ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Biological Basis and Tumor Microenvironment in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Biological Basis and Tumor Microenvironment in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A defining feature of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is the marked discrepancy between the scarcity of malignant Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells and the abundance of reactive non-malignant cells. This architecture reflects a biologically active tumor microenvironment in which neoplastic cells depend on surrounding T cells, macrophages, eosinophils, fibroblasts, and stromal elements for survival and immune protection rather than autonomous tumor mass expansion alone. Broad hematology overviews consistently emphasize that the clinical and pathological identity of cHL is inseparable from this microenvironmental dependence, which distinguishes it from many other lymphoid malignancies ref [9].

Functionally, the cHL microenvironment is sustained by reciprocal cytokine and chemokine signaling that attracts inflammatory and immunoregulatory populations while blunting effective anti-tumor immunity. The resulting milieu contributes not only to tumor persistence but also to systemic manifestations, including constitutional symptoms and prolonged fatigue, underscoring that cHL biology extends beyond the malignant clone itself ref [14]. In this context, therapeutic efficacy in relapsed disease after transplantation has also been interpreted as evidence that immune-mediated mechanisms can meaningfully reshape disease control, as illustrated by the benefit of reduced-intensity allogeneic approaches over conventional therapy in selected patients ref [16].

The importance of the tumor ecosystem in cHL has further influenced long-term thinking about treatment selection and survivorship. Standard lymphoma references increasingly frame disease biology together with host–tumor interactions when discussing modern therapeutic strategy ref [9]. At the same time, late toxicities after historical treatment, including radiation-associated second malignancies such as mesothelioma, highlight why biologically informed and more selective approaches are essential as the field moves from broad cytotoxic control toward targeted and immune-based modulation of the cHL microenvironment ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Biological Basis and Tumor Microenvironment in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Biological Basis and Tumor Microenvironment in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) provides an important biologic layer in a subset of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), helping explain how rare Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells acquire survival advantages within an otherwise hostile immune milieu. EBV-positive cHL is thought to exploit latent viral programs that promote NF-κB and related prosurvival signaling, while simultaneously shaping cytokine and chemokine networks that recruit and polarize nonmalignant immune cells. In this sense, EBV is not merely an associated finding, but a contributor to the distinctive cHL microenvironmental ecosystem ref [21].

From a translational perspective, EBV-related biomarkers have attracted interest for disease evaluation and monitoring. Circulating EBV DNA load has been explored as a surrogate of tumor burden and treatment response in EBV-associated lymphoid malignancies, with potential relevance in selected cHL cases, although its utility is necessarily confined to EBV-driven disease subsets rather than the broader cHL population ref [21]. These observations reinforce the concept that viral biology can complement tissue-based pathology in refining risk assessment and dynamic response evaluation.

The biologic boundaries of cHL are further highlighted by mediastinal gray zone lymphoma, an entity with overlapping clinicopathologic features of cHL and primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma. Its existence underscores that the signaling architecture and microenvironmental interactions typical of cHL may blend with features of adjacent lymphoma categories, particularly in mediastinal disease ref [33]. Recognizing such overlap is important for interpreting biomarker studies and for understanding why some tumors exhibit intermediate phenotypes, distinct immune niches, and divergent therapeutic behavior compared with conventional cHL ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Biological Basis and Tumor Microenvironment in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Biological Basis and Tumor Microenvironment in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A translationally important consequence of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) biology is the emergence of actionable biomarkers that link tumor-cell phenotype to therapeutic vulnerability. Among these, CD30 is the defining surface marker of Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells and has diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic relevance. Its consistent expression in cHL has made it both a disease classifier and a highly effective therapeutic target, providing the biological rationale for anti-CD30 strategies that have reshaped treatment in relapsed and frontline settings ref [24], ref [16].

Beyond CD30 itself, biomarker development in cHL increasingly reflects the interplay between malignant cells and the immune-rich microenvironment. Precision-medicine approaches incorporate immunophenotypic and molecular markers to refine diagnosis, distinguish cHL from overlapping entities, and identify patients most likely to benefit from targeted agents or immunotherapy. In this context, biomarker assessment is not merely descriptive; it helps translate the characteristic signaling dependencies and immune-evasion programs of cHL into clinically meaningful therapeutic decisions ref [20], ref [16].

Thus, the biological study of cHL has moved from recognizing Reed–Sternberg cells as rare diagnostic cells to understanding them as organizers of a permissive microenvironment and carriers of tractable surface and immune biomarkers. This shift underpins contemporary treatment development, in which CD30-directed therapy and biomarker-informed patient stratification exemplify how pathobiology has been converted into precision oncology for cHL ref [24], ref [20], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Presentation, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Staging
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Presentation, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Staging - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) most commonly presents with painless lymphadenopathy, typically involving cervical, supraclavicular, or mediastinal nodal regions, and may be accompanied by constitutional “B symptoms” including fever, drenching night sweats, and weight loss. Some patients also report pruritus, alcohol-induced nodal pain, fatigue, cough, chest discomfort, or dyspnea when bulky mediastinal disease is present. These presenting features are clinically important because they influence both initial suspicion and formal risk stratification at diagnosis ref [16], ref [39].

The initial clinical evaluation begins with careful history taking and physical examination, with attention to symptom duration, nodal distribution, bulky masses, performance status, and extranodal complaints. Baseline laboratory assessment typically includes complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver and renal function tests, and other routine biochemical studies that help characterize inflammatory burden, organ reserve, and potential treatment constraints. Diagnostic confirmation requires adequate tissue, and excisional lymph-node biopsy is generally preferred over limited sampling to preserve architecture and enable distinction of cHL from mimics and other lymphoma subtypes ref [16], ref [39].

Although these principles have remained stable across guideline iterations, modern practice increasingly integrates clinical findings with pathology and imaging from the outset to define disease extent and guide subsequent staging. Thus, the presenting syndrome in cHL is not merely descriptive; it forms the first layer of a risk-adapted diagnostic workflow that underpins treatment planning and follow-up strategy ref [16], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Presentation, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Staging
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Presentation, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Staging - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Diagnostic evaluation of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) begins with histologic confirmation from an adequate excisional or core biopsy, followed by integrated clinical, laboratory, and imaging assessment. Baseline workup typically includes complete blood counts, inflammatory markers, liver and renal function testing, and careful examination for nodal and extranodal disease burden. Cross-sectional imaging has largely been complemented by 18F-FDG PET/CT, which provides both anatomic and metabolic information for initial staging and subsequent response-adapted management in FDG-avid lymphomas such as cHL [3, 13].

For staging, PET/CT has become central because it improves detection of involved nodal stations and extranodal sites compared with conventional imaging alone, thereby refining Ann Arbor/Lugano classification and treatment planning [13]. In particular, PET/CT assessment of bone and bone marrow involvement has reduced reliance on routine bone marrow trephine biopsy in many patients, as metabolically active marrow lesions can be identified noninvasively with high clinical utility at diagnosis [16]. This shift is especially relevant in patients without cytopenias or other features strongly suggestive of discordant marrow pathology [13, 16].

Although diagnosis remains morphologic, prognostic evaluation increasingly incorporates features of the tumor microenvironment. At baseline, the expression of FOXP3, CD68, and CD20 in diagnostic specimens has been associated with outcome, underscoring that pathology in cHL extends beyond Reed–Sternberg cell identification to characterization of the surrounding immune infiltrate [15]. Thus, contemporary diagnostic evaluation is multidisciplinary, combining tissue pathology with PET/CT-based staging and selected biologic markers to support risk stratification and guide therapeutic intensity [3, 13, 15].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Presentation, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Staging
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Presentation, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Staging - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Diagnostic confirmation of classical Hodgkin lymphoma requires adequate tissue architecture and careful histopathologic correlation with the clinical and radiologic context. Excisional lymph-node biopsy remains the preferred approach because it best preserves nodal architecture and facilitates recognition of scattered Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells within the characteristic inflammatory background; core-needle biopsy may be considered when excision is impractical, but limited samples can hinder definitive subclassification or distinction from other lymphoid neoplasms ref [9].

When disease is located in deep or mediastinal sites, image-guided tissue sampling can provide a practical route to diagnosis. CT-guided core biopsy has shown useful diagnostic yield in malignant lymphoma and may reduce the need for more invasive surgical procedures, although nondiagnostic or insufficient samples still necessitate repeat biopsy in selected cases ref [28]. In routine evaluation, pathologic confirmation is integrated with baseline laboratory studies and cross-sectional imaging to define disease extent and identify factors relevant to treatment planning, including bulky disease, extranodal involvement, and systemic inflammatory burden ref [9].

Symptom assessment is also part of the initial diagnostic workup because constitutional manifestations influence staging and prognostic stratification. Beyond classic B symptoms, fatigue is a frequent and clinically meaningful complaint in Hodgkin lymphoma, both at presentation and during survivorship, and its longitudinal burden underscores the importance of documenting patient-reported symptoms alongside objective disease measures ref [14]. Thus, modern diagnostic evaluation in cHL is not limited to establishing histology; it also incorporates procedural strategy, anatomic mapping, laboratory assessment, and symptom characterization to support accurate staging and risk-adapted management ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Presentation, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Staging
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Presentation, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Staging - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Tissue confirmation remains the cornerstone of cHL diagnosis, because architectural assessment and immunophenotyping are required to distinguish cHL from reactive conditions, non-Hodgkin lymphomas, and mediastinal gray-zone entities. Excisional lymph node biopsy is preferred when feasible, but image-guided core needle biopsy can provide adequate diagnostic material in selected anatomical sites and is particularly useful when surgery is impractical or higher risk. In head and neck presentations, ultrasound-guided core biopsy has shown practical value as a minimally invasive diagnostic approach for lymphoma workup, provided that sufficient tissue is obtained for histology and ancillary studies [9].

A key procedural pitfall is prebiopsy corticosteroid exposure, especially in patients with bulky mediastinal disease. Corticosteroids may induce rapid tumor regression, obscure Reed-Sternberg cells, and compromise diagnostic accuracy, thereby delaying definitive classification and treatment planning. This issue is particularly relevant in symptomatic mediastinal presentations, where empiric steroid use for airway or compressive symptoms should be weighed carefully against the risk of nondiagnostic sampling and, when unavoidable, clearly documented for the pathologist and multidisciplinary team [6].

Beyond conventional biopsy, liquid biopsy is emerging as an adjunctive tool in lymphoma diagnostics and disease monitoring. Although it does not replace tissue diagnosis in cHL, circulating tumor DNA–based approaches may eventually help detect occult disease, refine molecular characterization, and support response assessment when repeat tissue sampling is difficult [34]. In current practice, therefore, the diagnostic workflow for suspected cHL should prioritize timely acquisition of adequate tissue, avoidance of pre-analytic factors that reduce yield, and selective incorporation of newer molecular assays as complementary rather than stand-alone tests [6,9,34].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Presentation, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Staging
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Presentation, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Staging - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Staging and risk stratification in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) have evolved from purely anatomic classification toward integrated clinicometabolic assessment. The Ann Arbor/Cotswolds framework remains the basis for defining limited versus advanced disease, incorporating nodal distribution, extranodal extension, and B symptoms, but contemporary practice increasingly combines these descriptors with bulk, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and PET-derived disease extent to guide treatment intensity ref [24], ref [25]. This shift reflects the need to distinguish patients suitable for de-escalated therapy from those requiring more intensive or response-adapted approaches.

FDG-PET/CT is now central to both baseline staging and early treatment adaptation. Compared with conventional CT, PET/CT improves detection of metabolically active nodal and extranodal sites, refines stage assignment, and can reduce the need for routine bone marrow biopsy in many patients with cHL when marrow involvement is not otherwise suspected ref [10], ref [16]. Interim PET has particular prognostic value, enabling escalation or de-escalation strategies based on early chemosensitivity, while end-of-treatment PET/CT supports response classification and residual mass interpretation ref [10], ref [25].

Prognostic modeling further complements stage. In pediatric disease, the Childhood Hodgkin International Prognostic Score (CHIPS) provides a practical pretreatment tool for estimating event-free survival and identifying higher-risk patients beyond anatomic stage alone ref [22]. More broadly, guideline-based evaluation emphasizes that prognostic assessment should integrate age group, clinical risk factors, pathology-confirmed diagnosis, and high-quality imaging rather than rely on a single variable ref [16], ref [25]. Because management decisions depend on accurate histologic classification, image-guided core needle biopsy may be appropriate in selected settings when excisional biopsy is impractical, provided adequate tissue is obtained for morphology and immunophenotyping ref [27].

subsections.section_title: Standard Therapeutic Strategies Across Disease Stages
subsections.subsection_title: Standard Therapeutic Strategies Across Disease Stages - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
For newly diagnosed classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), standard first-line management is fundamentally stage-adapted, with curative intent in the vast majority of patients. Contemporary guideline-based care stratifies treatment into limited-stage and advanced-stage disease, balancing disease control against late toxicity. Combination chemotherapy remains the backbone of therapy, while involved-site radiotherapy is selectively integrated according to stage, bulk, and response, rather than used uniformly as in earlier eras ref [16], ref [39].

In early-stage favorable disease, abbreviated anthracycline-based chemotherapy followed by carefully planned radiotherapy has historically provided excellent control, whereas early-stage unfavorable or bulky presentations generally require more intensive combined-modality treatment. In advanced-stage cHL, full-course systemic chemotherapy is standard, with radiotherapy reserved for selected residual or initially bulky sites. Across these settings, treatment selection increasingly reflects not only anatomic stage and conventional risk factors but also concern for long-term survivorship, especially when cure rates are high ref [16], ref [39].

These survivorship considerations are central to modern standard therapy. Long-term follow-up studies have shown substantial excess cardiovascular morbidity after HL treatment, including late coronary disease, valvular injury, and heart failure related to prior mediastinal irradiation and anthracycline exposure ref [9], ref [23], ref [37]. Likewise, gonadal dysfunction and impaired fertility remain important consequences of some chemotherapy strategies, particularly in younger patients expected to survive for decades ref [30]. Accordingly, current standard therapeutic planning aims not only to maximize initial cure but also to minimize cumulative cardiac, valvular, and reproductive toxicity through judicious selection of chemotherapy intensity and radiotherapy use ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Standard Therapeutic Strategies Across Disease Stages
subsections.subsection_title: Standard Therapeutic Strategies Across Disease Stages - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central component of stage-adapted management in newly diagnosed classical Hodgkin lymphoma is accurate baseline staging and early response assessment, because modern treatment intensity is increasingly modified according to metabolic imaging. FDG-PET/CT has become the key modality for defining nodal and extranodal disease burden, complementing contrast-enhanced anatomic imaging and enabling more precise assignment to limited-, intermediate-, or advanced-stage therapeutic pathways. In addition, PET-based response evaluation provides the framework for risk-adapted de-escalation or escalation after initial chemotherapy cycles, thereby refining the balance between disease control and long-term toxicity ref [13], ref [6].

In this context, PET-guided strategies have also reduced reliance on some older staging procedures. Bone marrow involvement in Hodgkin lymphoma is relatively uncommon and is often identifiable by FDG-PET/CT, which may obviate routine bone marrow trephine biopsy in many patients when imaging findings are clearly negative or diagnostically informative. This shift is clinically relevant because it streamlines staging while preserving accuracy and aligns with the broader movement toward imaging-driven therapeutic decision making in cHL ref [16], ref [13].

The practical implication is that standard first-line therapy is no longer determined solely by Ann Arbor stage, but by an integrated assessment of disease extent, bulk, risk features, and interim metabolic response. Such an approach supports the contemporary use of combined-modality therapy in selected early-stage patients, chemotherapy-alone strategies in others, and treatment intensification in patients with inadequate early PET response, all within a framework of minimizing late effects without compromising cure rates ref [6], ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Standard Therapeutic Strategies Across Disease Stages
subsections.subsection_title: Standard Therapeutic Strategies Across Disease Stages - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
In advanced-stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma, standard first-line management is centered on multi-agent chemotherapy, with treatment intensity tailored to disease burden, comorbidity, and expected late toxicity. Broad lymphoma treatment reviews describe ABVD as a longstanding backbone, while more intensive regimens are reserved for selected high-risk patients in whom disease control is prioritized over toxicity minimization; in this setting, response-adapted strategies increasingly seek to balance efficacy against cumulative pulmonary, cardiac, and fertility-related harms ref [9].

For advanced disease, radiotherapy is no longer applied routinely to all initial sites but is generally considered for residual masses or selected bulky presentations after systemic therapy. This restrained use reflects concern over late adverse effects among long-term survivors, including secondary thoracic malignancies after prior mediastinal irradiation, which has reinforced efforts to minimize unnecessary radiation exposure while preserving disease control ref [39]. General treatment overviews similarly position consolidative radiotherapy as a selective rather than universal component of stage-adapted care ref [9].

Risk-adapted management must also account for survivorship endpoints. Persistent fatigue is common during and after treatment and may substantially affect functional recovery, underscoring the importance of choosing regimens that avoid excess toxicity when oncologically appropriate and of integrating supportive care into frontline planning ref [14]. Accordingly, contemporary standard therapy across advanced stages is best viewed as a composite strategy: effective induction chemotherapy, selective use of radiotherapy, and continuous reassessment of long-term treatment burden in survivors ref [9][14][39].

subsections.section_title: Standard Therapeutic Strategies Across Disease Stages
subsections.subsection_title: Standard Therapeutic Strategies Across Disease Stages - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Special therapeutic populations require adaptation of standard cHL treatment principles to balance disease control against excess toxicity. In older or medically frail patients, anthracycline- and bleomycin-containing regimens may be poorly tolerated, making comorbidity assessment, baseline organ function, and competing mortality risks central to treatment selection. Although these concerns are well recognized across lymphoma practice, broader lymphoma guideline and outcomes literature also underscore that noncancer deaths and treatment-related morbidity substantially influence management intensity in vulnerable populations, supporting individualized rather than uniform escalation strategies ref [36], ref [11].

Patients with autoimmune disease, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, present an additional layer of complexity because pre-existing immune dysregulation, prior immunosuppressive exposure, and heightened susceptibility to infection may affect both treatment tolerance and diagnostic interpretation. While these data are not specific to cHL, population-based evidence linking rheumatoid arthritis and lymphoma risk highlights the need for careful multidisciplinary planning when standard chemotherapy is considered in such patients ref [37]. Similarly, when cHL arises in unusual extranodal contexts or enters the differential diagnosis alongside other aggressive lymphoma subtypes, lessons from extranodal B-cell and NK/T-cell lymphoma management emphasize the importance of site-specific toxicity considerations and tailored local–systemic integration rather than rigid protocol application ref [35], ref [38].

At the same time, therapeutic de-intensification may be appropriate in selected low-tolerance settings, whereas overt undertreatment should be avoided in fit patients. Experience from other indolent or biologically distinct lymphomas shows that observation or highly conservative approaches are appropriate only in narrowly defined circumstances and should not be extrapolated indiscriminately to symptomatic cHL ref [10]. Looking forward, supportive innovations—including drug-delivery platforms such as nanoparticles—may help improve therapeutic index in frail or toxicity-prone patients, although these remain investigational and not part of current frontline standard care ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Standard Therapeutic Strategies Across Disease Stages
subsections.subsection_title: Standard Therapeutic Strategies Across Disease Stages - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Special therapeutic situations in newly diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma require adaptation beyond standard stage-based algorithms. In pediatric disease, treatment seeks to preserve cure while minimizing late toxicity, and risk stratification tools such as the Childhood Hodgkin International Prognostic Score (CHIPS) help identify children at higher risk for relapse who may warrant treatment intensification or closer response-adapted monitoring ref [22]. PET/CT also has a central role in contemporary response assessment, supporting early modification of therapy and, in selected cases, reduction of radiotherapy exposure to limit long-term sequelae ref [10].

Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma represents a biologically and clinically distinct entity and should not simply be managed as classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Its generally indolent behavior, CD20 expression, and tendency toward late relapse justify individualized approaches that may include limited-field radiotherapy alone for localized disease, anti-CD20-based strategies, or carefully selected observation rather than routine cHL-type combined-modality therapy in every patient ref [15]. Broader adult treatment overviews and guideline statements likewise emphasize tailoring frontline management to age, comorbidity, histologic subtype, and treatment tolerance, particularly in older or frail patients in whom standard intensive regimens may be poorly tolerated ref [16], ref [25].

These decisions should also be informed by survivorship considerations. Health-related quality-of-life data show that fatigue, psychosocial impairment, and treatment-related late effects remain substantial even among cured patients, reinforcing the importance of de-escalation strategies when oncologically safe and of supportive care throughout therapy ref [18]. Thus, special populations in Hodgkin lymphoma are best managed through a personalized framework that integrates disease biology, PET-guided response, anticipated toxicity, and long-term quality-of-life outcomes ref [10], ref [18].

subsections.section_title: Relapsed/Refractory Disease and Emerging Therapeutic Innovations
subsections.subsection_title: Relapsed/Refractory Disease and Emerging Therapeutic Innovations - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Relapsed or refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) remains a pivotal therapeutic challenge, particularly in patients who fail to achieve durable remission after frontline combined-modality therapy. Contemporary management begins with reassessment of disease extent, prior treatment exposure, performance status, and chemosensitivity, because these factors determine eligibility for curative-intent salvage strategies. ESMO guidance has consistently positioned second-line chemotherapy followed by high-dose therapy and autologous stem-cell transplantation (ASCT) as the standard approach for fit patients with transplant-eligible relapse, while recognizing that primary refractory disease and early relapse portend less favorable outcomes than late recurrence ref [16], ref [39].

In this conventional paradigm, the principal objective of salvage treatment is not only cytoreduction but also demonstration of treatment responsiveness before ASCT. Guideline-based algorithms therefore emphasize individualized selection of salvage regimens and close response assessment, with transplantation remaining the backbone of therapy for patients with chemosensitive disease ref [16], ref [39]. For patients who relapse after ASCT, are ineligible for transplantation, or have multiply relapsed disease, historical outcomes with conventional treatment alone have been poor, prompting consideration of alternative consolidative or immune-based approaches, including allogeneic transplantation in selected cases ref [16], ref [39].

Thus, the relapsed/refractory setting in cHL illustrates the broader evolution of the field: from uniform chemotherapy-centered salvage toward risk-adapted sequencing of transplantation, targeted agents, and immunotherapy. This shift does not eliminate the importance of established standards, but rather reframes ASCT as one component within an increasingly nuanced therapeutic continuum for biologically and clinically heterogeneous relapse patterns ref [16], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Relapsed/Refractory Disease and Emerging Therapeutic Innovations
subsections.subsection_title: Relapsed/Refractory Disease and Emerging Therapeutic Innovations - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Response assessment and biologic risk stratification are central to contemporary management of relapsed/refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma, particularly when selecting candidates for salvage therapy and transplantation. FDG-PET/CT has become the key imaging modality for defining metabolically active relapse, evaluating chemosensitivity before autologous transplantation, and distinguishing residual fibrosis from viable disease, thereby refining treatment sequencing beyond conventional anatomic imaging alone [ref 13]. More broadly, modern reviews of Hodgkin lymphoma emphasize that outcomes after relapse are closely linked to depth of response before transplant-based consolidation, underscoring the value of accurate functional imaging in this setting [ref 3].

Although primarily developed for initial staging, PET-based marrow assessment also illustrates the broader transition toward less invasive, response-adapted disease evaluation. Evidence that FDG-PET/CT can identify bone and bone marrow involvement with high clinical utility supports its role in comprehensive disease reassessment and may reduce reliance on procedures such as marrow biopsy when relapse is being re-evaluated [ref 16]. In parallel, imaging-centered lymphoma guidelines reinforce PET/CT as the preferred platform for both staging and treatment-response interpretation, which is particularly relevant when deciding whether patients have achieved a sufficiently favorable remission state to proceed to transplant or alternative systemic strategies [ref 13].

Biologic features of the tumor microenvironment may further refine risk assessment in the relapsed setting. Diagnostic expression patterns of FOXP3, CD68, and CD20 in classical Hodgkin lymphoma have been associated with differential outcomes, suggesting that host-tumor interactions influence treatment sensitivity and may help identify subgroups likely to benefit from targeted or immunologically oriented approaches [ref 15]. This concept is supported by the phase II experience with rituximab in relapsed CD20-positive Hodgkin lymphoma, which demonstrated that biomarker-defined subsets can derive clinically meaningful benefit from antibody-based therapy with acceptable tolerability [ref 17]. Together, these observations support an emerging paradigm in which PET-defined response and microenvironmental or phenotypic markers jointly guide increasingly personalized salvage treatment [ref 3].

subsections.section_title: Relapsed/Refractory Disease and Emerging Therapeutic Innovations
subsections.subsection_title: Relapsed/Refractory Disease and Emerging Therapeutic Innovations - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
For patients with classical Hodgkin lymphoma who relapse after autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT), prognosis has historically been poor and conventional non-transplant approaches have offered limited durability. In this setting, reduced-intensity conditioning allogeneic stem cell transplantation (RIC-alloSCT) emerged as a strategy intended to extend disease control while reducing the prohibitive treatment-related mortality associated with myeloablative allografting. The rationale is particularly compelling in post-ASCT failure, where further cytotoxic salvage alone is rarely curative and a graft-versus-lymphoma effect may provide clinically meaningful benefit [16].

The available comparative evidence suggests that RIC-alloSCT can outperform conventional treatment after relapse following ASCT, supporting its role in selected fit patients with chemosensitive disease and an appropriate donor. This benefit must, however, be balanced against persistent risks of graft-versus-host disease, infectious complications, and non-relapse mortality, which continue to limit universal applicability. Accordingly, patient selection remains central, with disease status at transplant, prior treatment burden, comorbidity, and donor availability all influencing expected benefit [16].

In the modern era, the place of alloSCT is being redefined rather than eliminated. Novel agents such as antibody-drug conjugates and checkpoint inhibitors have improved pre-transplant disease control and may serve as bridges to transplantation, whereas some patients now achieve sufficiently durable remissions to defer or avoid alloSCT. Nevertheless, for multiply relapsed or refractory cHL—particularly after ASCT failure—RIC-alloSCT remains an important consolidative option within an increasingly individualized treatment algorithm, representing the interface between historical salvage paradigms and contemporary immune-based therapy [16].

subsections.section_title: Relapsed/Refractory Disease and Emerging Therapeutic Innovations
subsections.subsection_title: Relapsed/Refractory Disease and Emerging Therapeutic Innovations - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
An important frontier in relapsed/refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma is the integration of response monitoring with treatment personalization. Liquid biopsy approaches, including circulating tumor DNA and other blood-based molecular assays, offer a minimally invasive means to detect residual disease, characterize clonal evolution, and potentially identify impending relapse earlier than conventional clinical progression. In lymphoma more broadly, these platforms are being developed for disease genotyping, longitudinal surveillance, and treatment-response assessment, making them attractive adjuncts to PET/CT in the salvage setting and during post-transplant or post-immunotherapy follow-up ref [34].

Beyond monitoring, emerging delivery technologies may expand the therapeutic index of novel agents in heavily pretreated disease. Nanoparticle-based systems are being explored to improve drug solubility, tumor targeting, intracellular delivery, and controlled release, with the broader goal of enhancing antitumor efficacy while limiting systemic toxicity. In leukemia and lymphoma models, such platforms have been proposed for chemotherapeutic payloads, biologics, and combination strategies, suggesting a future role in overcoming resistance or reducing cumulative treatment burden in cHL salvage therapy ref [7].

Together, these innovations support a shift from empiric retreatment toward adaptive, precision-guided care. Liquid biopsy may refine risk stratification and enable earlier therapeutic intervention, whereas nanotechnology-based drug delivery could help optimize exposure to active agents in multiply relapsed patients. Although both approaches remain largely investigational in cHL, they exemplify how biomarker-driven surveillance and engineered therapeutics may complement established transplantation, antibody-drug conjugate, and checkpoint inhibitor paradigms in the next generation of relapse management ref [34], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Relapsed/Refractory Disease and Emerging Therapeutic Innovations
subsections.subsection_title: Relapsed/Refractory Disease and Emerging Therapeutic Innovations - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A central future direction in relapsed/refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is the move from empiric salvage toward biomarker-informed, response-adapted therapy. CD30 remains the most established actionable marker in cHL, providing both diagnostic confirmation and a therapeutic anchor for antibody-based strategies, while broader biomarker programs increasingly seek to refine risk stratification, predict drug sensitivity, and identify mechanisms of immune escape or resistance ref [15], ref [20]. In this framework, relapsed disease is no longer viewed as a uniform clinical state but as a biologically heterogeneous setting requiring individualized sequencing of transplantation, anti-CD30 therapy, and immunotherapy ref [16].

Functional imaging is integral to this precision-oriented approach. PET/CT not only defines chemosensitivity before autologous transplantation but also helps determine whether additional salvage, consolidation, or a switch in systemic strategy is warranted, thereby serving as a practical bridge between biologic risk and therapeutic decision-making ref [10]. Contemporary guideline-based care similarly incorporates PET-guided assessment together with prior treatment exposure, remission duration, and transplant eligibility when selecting subsequent therapy for relapsed/refractory cHL ref [25].

Looking ahead, the convergence of CD30-directed therapeutics, immune checkpoint modulation, and predictive biomarkers is likely to reshape treatment algorithms beyond the historical chemotherapy-transplant paradigm. The major challenge is not merely expanding the therapeutic armamentarium, but identifying which patients require intensification, which can avoid cumulative toxicity, and which should be directed early to novel combinations or clinical trials. Thus, the future management of relapsed/refractory cHL will depend on integrating molecular biomarkers, immune contexture, and PET-defined response into a coherent precision-medicine model ref [15], ref [20], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Long-Term Outcomes, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Long-Term Outcomes, Survivorship, and Future Directions - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Because most patients with classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) are cured, long-term outcome assessment must extend beyond relapse-free survival to encompass treatment-related morbidity and competing causes of death. Survivorship studies have shown that cardiovascular disease emerges as a major determinant of late health burden, with risk persisting and accumulating for decades after therapy, particularly among individuals exposed to mediastinal radiotherapy and anthracycline-containing regimens ref [9], ref [37]. Current follow-up guidance therefore emphasizes structured long-term surveillance, risk-factor modification, and attention to late effects as integral components of cHL care rather than optional adjuncts ref [16].

Among cardiovascular sequelae, the spectrum is broad and includes coronary disease, heart failure, and clinically significant valvular injury. Long-term cohort analyses demonstrate substantial excess cardiovascular risk up to 40 years after treatment ref [9]. Dose-related associations between cardiac radiation exposure and anthracycline use have also clarified the mechanistic basis for late heart failure in survivors ref [37]. In parallel, valvular heart disease represents a distinct and important late complication after Hodgkin lymphoma treatment, reinforcing the need for prolonged cardiac monitoring even in apparently disease-free survivors ref [23].

Survivorship also includes preservation of reproductive health and quality of life in younger patients. Data from the German Hodgkin Study Group trials indicate that gonadal dysfunction and impaired fertility remain relevant late effects, with risk shaped by treatment intensity and modality ref [30]. These observations support contemporary efforts to refine therapy using response-adapted and biologically informed approaches that maintain cure rates while reducing cumulative exposure to cardiotoxic and gonadotoxic treatment components ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Long-Term Outcomes, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Long-Term Outcomes, Survivorship, and Future Directions - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central survivorship challenge in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is the need to sustain high cure rates while reducing treatment intensity in patients who are likely to do well. Contemporary management has increasingly relied on response-adapted imaging, particularly PET/CT, to refine risk during therapy and to support de-escalation strategies that may lessen cumulative exposure to radiation and cytotoxic chemotherapy without compromising disease control in selected patients ref [13]. In this context, long-term outcome assessment should not be limited to relapse-free survival, but should incorporate the consequences of treatment tailoring for late morbidity, functional status, and quality of survivorship ref [5], ref [13].

Risk stratification may also be improved by biological features present at diagnosis. Microenvironmental markers such as FOXP3-, CD68-, and CD20-associated patterns have been linked to outcome in cHL, suggesting that baseline immune contexture contains prognostic information beyond conventional clinical staging ref [15]. Although such biomarkers are not yet standard tools for survivorship planning, they point toward a future in which frontline treatment intensity, follow-up schedules, and supportive interventions are informed by both tumor biology and host factors rather than by anatomical burden alone ref [15], ref [5].

Future research should therefore integrate imaging-based response assessment with biologically informed prognostication to identify patients who can safely receive less intensive therapy and those who remain at higher risk for relapse or treatment-related harm ref [13], ref [15]. For long-term survivors, this approach could enable more individualized follow-up focused on toxicity surveillance, second cancer prevention, and restoration of physical and psychosocial well-being, aligning cHL care with a broader survivorship model rather than an exclusively disease-centered paradigm ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Long-Term Outcomes, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Long-Term Outcomes, Survivorship, and Future Directions - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central survivorship challenge in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is the persistence of patient-reported symptoms long after remission, particularly fatigue and sexual dysfunction. Longitudinal data from the German Hodgkin Study Group show that cancer-related fatigue can remain clinically relevant during and after treatment, underscoring that cure does not necessarily equate to full functional recovery and that survivorship assessment should extend beyond conventional disease endpoints ref [14]. In parallel, studies of male sexuality after cancer treatment indicate substantial unmet needs for information and support among lymphoma survivors, highlighting the importance of integrating sexual health counseling, fertility discussion, and psychosocial care into routine follow-up ref [34].

Late toxicity surveillance must also account for rare but severe treatment-related second malignancies. Radiation-associated malignant mesothelioma, although uncommon, exemplifies the long latency and seriousness of secondary cancers that may emerge years after curative therapy for Hodgkin lymphoma ref [39]. These observations reinforce the rationale for modern treatment de-escalation, field reduction, and survivorship programs tailored to prior treatment exposures, symptom burden, and quality-of-life priorities ref [14], ref [39].

Future directions should therefore combine durable disease control with minimization of cumulative toxicity. For patients relapsing after autologous transplantation, reduced-intensity allogeneic transplantation has been reported to offer superior outcomes compared with conventional approaches in selected settings, illustrating how salvage strategies may preserve curative intent while reshaping the long-term risk profile ref [16]. More broadly, survivorship-oriented cHL research should prioritize prospective patient-reported outcomes, sexual and endocrine health, and exposure-adapted follow-up so that therapeutic success is measured not only by survival, but also by sustained well-being ref [14], ref [16], ref [34].

subsections.section_title: Long-Term Outcomes, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Long-Term Outcomes, Survivorship, and Future Directions - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A forward-looking survivorship agenda in classical Hodgkin lymphoma should increasingly rely on longitudinal real-world data infrastructures. Population-based registries can complement clinical trials by capturing late relapse, second malignancies, treatment-related organ toxicity, and patterns of long-term healthcare use across broader and more heterogeneous patient populations than are typically enrolled in prospective studies. The Danish National Lymphoma Registry illustrates the value of such systematic, nationwide data collection for outcome surveillance, benchmarking, and hypothesis generation in lymphoma care ref [38].

An important conceptual shift is to evaluate success not only by disease control, but also by the balance between cancer-specific mortality and competing noncancer causes of death. Although focused on diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, cure-fraction and cause-specific mortality modeling provides a useful framework for cHL survivorship research, where many patients live long enough for cardiovascular, pulmonary, and other late effects to shape overall prognosis. Such approaches may help define when patients can be considered functionally cured and identify subgroups in whom noncancer mortality becomes the dominant long-term risk ref [11].

Future directions also include minimally invasive monitoring strategies that could refine follow-up intensity and reduce cumulative diagnostic burden. Liquid biopsy platforms, including circulating tumor DNA-based assays, are being developed for lymphoma detection, response assessment, and molecular surveillance, with the potential to identify residual disease or relapse earlier than conventional approaches in selected settings ref [34]. For cHL survivors, integrating registry-based survivorship data with molecular monitoring may enable more individualized follow-up pathways, reserving intensive surveillance for those at highest biological and clinical risk while limiting unnecessary investigations and treatment-related anxiety in others refs [34, 38].

subsections.section_title: Long-Term Outcomes, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Long-Term Outcomes, Survivorship, and Future Directions - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Future directions in classical Hodgkin lymphoma should move beyond a singular focus on cure rates toward survivorship-informed, risk-adapted care. Contemporary treatment paradigms already incorporate PET/CT to refine response assessment and de-escalate or intensify therapy, providing a framework for reducing unnecessary exposure while preserving efficacy; this imaging-driven strategy is central to minimizing late cardiovascular, endocrine, fertility, and secondary malignant complications in long-term survivors ref [10]. Broader reviews of adult cHL management similarly emphasize that the next phase of progress will depend on biologically guided personalization rather than uniform escalation of treatment intensity ref [16].

A patient-centered future also requires systematic integration of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) into routine care and trial design. Evidence synthesized across HL populations shows that fatigue, psychosocial distress, impaired physical functioning, and social reintegration challenges may persist long after remission, underscoring that survival alone is an incomplete endpoint ref [18]. Accordingly, survivorship programs should incorporate longitudinal HRQoL monitoring, fertility counseling, cardiovascular risk surveillance, and supportive interventions as standard components of care rather than optional adjuncts ref [18], ref [16].

In pediatric and adolescent populations, future refinement of therapy is likely to depend on combining clinical risk models with response-adapted strategies. The Childhood Hodgkin International Prognostic Score (CHIPS) demonstrates the value of baseline prognostic stratification for predicting event-free survival, supporting efforts to identify children who may benefit from treatment reduction and those who require closer monitoring or novel approaches ref [22]. Together, prognostic modeling, PET-adapted response assessment, and survivorship-focused endpoints define a forward-looking research agenda aimed at maximizing cure while minimizing the lifelong burden of treatment ref [22], ref [10], ref [18].
